cards.front: Effective Java Item 10 — which property of the equals contract is most often violated?
cards.back: Symmetry — a.equals(b) must agree with b.equals(a)
cards.extra: A subclass that adds a field and compares it breaks symmetry against the base class. The book's example is a Point and a case-insensitive String.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 10 — when should you not override equals?
cards.back: When identity is the right meaning — each instance is inherently unique, or you never need value comparison
cards.extra: Overriding equals forces you into hashCode, immutability and symmetry questions. If value equality is not needed, leave the inherited identity version.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 10 — what must x.equals(null) return?
cards.back: false, never an exception
cards.extra: The contract requires it. A correct implementation checks instanceof first, which is null-safe and handles the type test in one step.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 11 — what breaks if you override equals but not hashCode?
cards.back: HashMap and HashSet — equal objects land in different buckets, so lookups fail
cards.extra: The contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes. The reverse is not required, and collisions are expected.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 11 — how do you write a correct hashCode?
cards.back: Start from a constant, combine each significant field's hash, and let the result overflow naturally
cards.extra: Modern answer: Objects.hash(...) or an IDE-generated version; the point is that every field used in equals must contribute.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 12 — what is wrong with the default toString?
cards.back: It prints ClassName@1b6d3586 — useless in logs, IDE debuggers and error messages
cards.extra: The contract asks for a concise but informative representation. Overriding it makes failures readable.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 13 — why does Effective Java call Cloneable broken?
cards.back: It has no clone method, and Object's clone is protected — so implementing it may still leave you unable to call it
cards.extra: The book's advice: prefer a copy constructor or copy factory. Implement clone only if you must, and then deep-copy mutable fields.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 14 — what does implementing Comparable declare?
cards.back: That instances have a natural ordering
cards.extra: It enables Arrays.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap and max/min without a Comparator.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 14 — what is the usual bug in a compareTo implementation?
cards.back: Using < or subtraction — overflow and wrong sign for negatives
cards.extra: Return negative, zero or positive. Integer.compare does it correctly; subtraction overflows.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 15 — what does Effective Java call the single most important factor in component quality?
cards.back: Minimising accessibility — every public member is a commitment
cards.extra: Start private and widen only with reason: private → package → protected → public. Each step exposes more of your design.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 15 — what is wrong with a public static final array field?
cards.back: It is mutable — clients can write into it
cards.extra: Arrays are always mutable, so a public static final array is a back door into your state. Return a defensive copy, or use List.of.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 16 — why prefer accessor methods to public fields in a public class?
cards.back: You cannot change the representation, enforce invariants, or take action on access
cards.extra: Once a field is public it is part of the API. Accessors keep the storage private and leave room to change it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 17 — what are the five rules for making a class immutable?
cards.back: No mutators; the class is final; all fields final and private; no mutable component escapes; defensive copies on the way in
cards.extra: Immutable instances are thread-safe by construction and can be shared freely.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::01 Classes and Objects

cards.front: Effective Java Item 18 — why does inheritance from a concrete, non-final class lead to fragile software?
cards.back: The subclass depends on the superclass's implementation details, which may change in a later release
cards.extra: The book's example: extending HashSet to count additions breaks when a future version adds an internal call to add.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 18 — what is the fix for that fragility?
cards.back: Composition: wrap the class and forward the calls you choose to expose
cards.extra: A wrapper does not depend on internals, and its API is yours. It is the decorator pattern applied to reuse.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 19 — what must a class that is designed for inheritance document?
cards.back: Its self-use of overridable methods — which methods call which, so subclasses know the consequences
cards.extra: Without that contract, subclasses override something innocuous and break invariants. The alternative is to forbid subclassing.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 19 — why must a constructor never call an overridable method?
cards.back: The override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised
cards.extra: Late binding applies during construction, so the override sees null/0. The book calls this a direct route to obscure failures.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 20 — why prefer an interface to an abstract class for defining a type?
cards.back: A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class
cards.extra: Interfaces also let an existing class be retrofitted by implementing the interface, with no new superclass.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 20 — what is a skeletal implementation class for?
cards.back: To give implementors the convenience of an abstract class while the type stays an interface
cards.extra: AbstractCollection is the pattern: the interface defines the type, the skeletal class carries the boilerplate.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::11 Abstraction

cards.front: Effective Java Item 21 — why is adding a method to a published interface dangerous, even with default methods?
cards.back: Existing implementations may inherit a default that does not hold their invariants
cards.extra: A default is a silent behaviour change. The book's advice: design interfaces for posterity and keep them small.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 22 — what is a constant interface and why is it wrong?
cards.back: An interface that only declares constants, so implementors can use them unqualified
cards.extra: It exposes implementation detail as API and pollutes the class's type hierarchy. Use an enum or a non-instantiable utility class.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Interfaces

cards.front: Effective Java Item 23 — why prefer a class hierarchy to a tagged class?
cards.back: A tag field means the object's behaviour depends on a field, so the type system cannot check it
cards.extra: Subclasses give per-flavour behaviour, compile-time checking and room to grow.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::12 Inheritance

cards.front: Effective Java Item 24 — why prefer static member classes to nonstatic ones?
cards.back: A nonstatic inner class keeps a hidden reference to its outer instance
cards.extra: That reference keeps the outer object alive, which is a classic leak when inner objects are handed out. Use static unless you need the outer instance.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::05 Nested Classes

cards.front: Effective Java Item 25 — why put one top-level class per source file?
cards.back: Multiple top-level classes in one file can provide multiple definitions, and which one is used depends on the classpath
cards.extra: Nothing is gained and compilation order can silently decide behaviour. One file, one top-level type.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::18 Packages
